source.title: Reinforcement Learning on Pre-Training Data

record.file_problem: The paper is present through its references, but some figure text is garbled or flattened, so numerical values in the scaling plots cannot be reliably read.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream benchmark performance across RLPT training-token scale, a different measure and training setup from the original held-out-loss scaling studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports downstream performance scaling with training tokens in Figure 1. Its general and mathematical benchmark comparisons in Tables 1 and 2 do not vary scale and are not separate scaling results. Figure 3 reports scaling trends for RLPT followed by RLVR, but the extracted figure is garbled and the text provides only an aggregate description; it is not recorded as a separate set of dataset-specific numerical rows.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper whose only scaling result is Figure 1. It shows downstream benchmark scores rising with RLPT training tokens, with fitted curves per benchmark. That is a new setting (RL on pre-training data, not next-token pretraining) with a result on V6. There is no loss, model-size or compute-allocation scaling, and no held-out extrapolation test, so the evidence is weak and in-sample only.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors say RLPT improves general and math benchmarks across Qwen3-4B/8B and Llama-3.2-3B. They say downstream performance 'follows a power-law decay' with training tokens (described as training compute), suggesting further gains with more compute. RLPT also strengthens subsequent RLVR.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales reinforcement learning on pre-training data and plots downstream benchmark scores against training tokens; it does not measure the original studies’ held-out next-token loss or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The scaling evidence is presented in figures whose extracted text is garbled, preventing reliable recovery of plotted values and fitted equations. The study does not report uncertainty for these scaling results or test held-out pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3 has a scaling plot for RLPT followed by RLVR, but its extracted chart is garbled and the paper describes only aggregate trends rather than reliably assignable values by benchmark and training step. The numerical rows from that figure were therefore not extracted.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
No fit-then-extrapolate test to larger runs.
Scales an RL regime but reports no loss curve. Whether the same power-law form holds is not tested beyond the downstream fits recorded under V6.
Untested parts: predictability from pretraining loss; scaling with model size; out-of-sample prediction; uncertainty of the fits.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents. Note that the fitted curve form is itself non-power-law.

missing.what: Figure 3: Pass@1/Pass@8 vs training step for RLVR alone vs RLPT+RLVR on MATH-500, AMC23, Minerva, AIME24 and AIME25. It is described only as 'consistent improvements throughout training'.

record.verdict_notes: Weak evidence for V6. The scale axis is RL training tokens on a fixed model, not pretraining scale. The fitted form a·exp(b·x^c) is a saturating curve, not a pure power law, despite the authors' wording. There is no held-out validation of the fits. Table 1 spans 3B–8B models, but these come from different families and the differences are not analysed as scaling, so no rows are needed.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The study uses an RL training regime on pre-training data, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds for held-out loss in other modalities or training regimes.
The study plots downstream benchmark performance against RLPT training tokens; it does not test predictability from pretraining loss or on a broad range of downstream-task types beyond those shown.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices, and systematic departures from a single power law.

rows.note: The authors state that performance on the benchmarks in Figure 1 follows a power-law decay with training tokens. The plotted values and fitted equation are not reliably recoverable from the extracted figure text.
rows.check: Subject not stated; most likely Qwen3-4B-Base, the main model, but the paper never says. A fitted equation is partly legible (MMLU: y≈105.6·exp(−0.300·x^−0.029), signs garbled). This is a saturating stretched-exponential form, not a pure power law, even though the authors call it 'power-law decay'.

relationships.condition: One unstated model (likely Qwen3-4B-Base) under RLPT; 9 general and math benchmarks vs RLPT training tokens (Figure 1)
relationships.reason: The authors fit smooth monotone curves to accuracy and Pass@1 vs training tokens on all nine benchmarks. The fits are in-sample only, with no uncertainty and no extrapolation test (R1–R9).
relationships.display_finding: Smooth monotone curves fitted accuracy and Pass@1 across all nine benchmarks, without uncertainty estimates or extrapolation tests.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The downstream benchmarks plotted in Figure 1 under RLPT training-token scaling
reader_labels.reason: The authors describe the benchmark performance as following a power-law trend with training tokens, consistent with predictable downstream improvement as scale increases (R1–R9).
